chunks: From him, from Amr ibn Uthman, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Ali ibn Ri'ab, from Abu Basir, who said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a man who married four women in one contract, or he said in one session, and their dowries were different. He said: 'It is permissible for him and for them.'

I said: What do you think if he went to some of the lands, and divorced one of the four, and bore witness upon her divorce by a group from the people of that land, while they did not know the woman? Then he married a woman from the people of that land after the expiration of the waiting period of the one he divorced, then he died after having consummated the marriage with her. How is his inheritance divided?

He said: 'If he has a child, then the woman whom he married last from the people of that land is entitled to one-fourth of one-eighth of what he left. And if the one who was divorced from the four is known by her very self and her lineage, then she has nothing from the inheritance, and upon her is the waiting period.'

And he said: 'The three women will divide three-fourths of one-eighth of what he left, and upon them is the waiting period. And if the one who was divorced from the four is not known, the four women will divide three-fourths of one-eighth of what he left among all of them, and upon all of them is the waiting period.'

key_terms.بِعَيْنِهَا وَ نَسَبِهَا: by her very self and her lineage

ai.seo_question: How is inheritance divided among four wives when one is divorced and her identity is uncertain?
ai.summary: This hadith from Al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib* elucidates the complex inheritance mechanics for a man who married four women simultaneously and later divorced one while traveling, creating a scenario of uncertainty regarding her identity. Imam al-Sadiq (AS) provides precise rulings on how the remaining wives and the newly married woman share the estate, distinguishing between cases where the divorced wife is identifiable by lineage versus those where she is not. This highlights the Shia juristic emphasis on the 'iddah' (waiting period) status and the evidentiary requirements for establishing marital rights in inheritance distribution.
